fields.Front: Why build a model before building the database, and what blueprint examples does the instructor use?
fields.Back: Build something large, make a mistake, and all that time is wasted; looking at a model first 'gets rid of a lot of the errors'. Her blueprints: the Wright brothers' original plane, a building blueprint with measurements and a visualization, and a baby gate.

fields.Front: List the five steps for figuring out what data to store in a large system (the objective asks for two).
fields.Back:
1. Gather all the reports the customers use, print or generate (e.g. a hospital 'number of falls' report)
2. Look at the screens where they enter, delete or modify data (a patient-entry screen with names, date of death, lab details, SSN)
3. Find the requirements of customers and stakeholders and write the specs
4. Figure out how they VIEW the data
5. Integrate the views to get the minimal data to store

fields.Front: Why integrate the users' overlapping views of the data?
fields.Back: So each piece of data is stored ONCE rather than twice for two different users; the code that accesses it then gets it from that one spot. Overlaps are exactly what you look for.

fields.Front: Give two reasons the instructor says an ER diagram is useful.
fields.Back:
1. It can be read without knowing any code, so you can sit down with your users, show them the diagram and they will understand it.
2. It is independent of any DBMS; once finished you MAP it to a real model - the relational model is the most common, but you could map it to others. (That mapping is Week 2.)

fields.Front: Name three tools for drawing ER diagrams, with one fact about each.
fields.Back:
Microsoft Visio: probably free for Western students, and it can help convert your ER diagram into a relational database.
draw.io (diagrams.net): online and free; used in every demonstration in the videos.
SmartDraw: requires signing up; ships example diagrams (banking, internet sales).

fields.Front: State the running case study (the COMPANY database) in its essentials.
fields.Back: A company organized into departments. Each department has a unique name, number and an employee who manages it (keep track of when they started managing); a department may have several locations. A department controls projects; each project has a unique number, name and a single location. Each employee has name, SSN, address, salary, sex, birthdate; is assigned to one department but may work on several projects (keep the hours on each); keep each employee's direct supervisor and their dependents (name, sex, birthdate, relation).

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §3.1): name the four phases of database design and say which are DBMS-independent.
fields.Back:
1. REQUIREMENTS COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: interview prospective users and document their DATA REQUIREMENTS; in parallel specify the FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS, the user-defined operations or transactions (retrievals and updates) the application will run.
2. CONCEPTUAL DESIGN: build the CONCEPTUAL SCHEMA in a high-level data model - the ER diagram. It contains no implementation details, which is why you can show it to a non-technical user. This phase also confirms the schema can answer the functional requirements.
3. LOGICAL DESIGN, also called DATA MODEL MAPPING: transform it into the implementation model of a specific DBMS - Week 2's seven rules. Often automated in design tools.
4. PHYSICAL DESIGN: internal storage structures, file organizations, indexes, access paths; application programs are implemented in parallel.
Phases 1 and 2 are DBMS-INDEPENDENT; phases 3 and 4 are DBMS-SPECIFIC. That split is the whole reason the ER model exists.

fields.Text: 'From this day forward, I want you to think about your {{c1::data}} before you ever think how you're going to {{c1::code}} something.' Always gather your {{c1::data}} first - this is the mindset Assignment 1 tests.
The Entity-Relationship model was created by {{c1::Peter Chen}} in {{c1::1976}}; an ER diagram is 'just a {{c1::visualization of your data}}'.

Two requirements-gathering steps: gather all the {{c1::reports}} the customers use or print, and look at the {{c1::screens}} where they enter, delete or modify data; then integrate the users' {{c1::views}} so each piece of data is stored once.
